## Proposition 10.100
**Statement:** The square on a minor straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth a fourth apotome.

**Step 1.** Let m be the given minor straight line and r the given rational straight line. Write x² for the square on x and xy for the rectangle contained by x and y. By the characterization of a minor, there are straight lines a > b such that m = a − b, the squares a² and b² are incommensurable, a² + b² is rational, and ab is medial (10.76). Consequently a + b is major (10.39). Our path is to apply 10.63 to this associated major, obtaining the square-excess condition required for a fourth apotome.

**Step 2.** Construct positive straight lines U and h such that
rU = a² + b² and rh = ab.
These applications are obtainable by fourth proportionals (6.12, 6.16), adding the breadths of the applications of a² and b² for the first equality (2.1). Since a² + b² is rational, U is rational and commensurable in length with r (10.20). Since ab is medial, h is rational and incommensurable in length with r (10.22).

**Step 3.** Put V = 2h. Then rV = 2ab (2.1). Also V² = 4h² (2.4), so V is rational: any area measuring both h² and the square on the assigned rational straight line also measures V² (D10.1.1, D10.1.3). Since h measures V, these two straight lines are commensurable in length; therefore V, like h, is incommensurable in length with r (D10.1.1, 10.13).

**Step 4.** By 2.7,
a² + b² = (a − b)² + 2ab.
Thus rU = m² + rV, and rU is greater than rV (CN5). Rectangles with the same height are proportional to their bases, so U > V (6.1, 5.14). Subtracting rV and using the distributivity of rectangles gives
r(U − V) = m²
(CN3, 2.1). Hence U − V is the breadth produced by applying the square on m to r.

**Step 5.** Since U and V are rational, their squares are commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line, and therefore with one another (D10.1.3, 10.12). But U is commensurable in length with r, whereas V is incommensurable in length with r; hence U and V are incommensurable in length (10.13). They are therefore rational straight lines commensurable in square only. It follows that U + V is binomial (10.36), and, since U > V, U − V is an apotome whose whole is U and whose annex is V (10.73).

**Step 6.** By 2.4 and 2.1,
(a + b)² = a² + b² + 2ab = rU + rV = r(U + V).
Thus U + V is the breadth obtained by applying the square on the major straight line a + b to r. It is consequently a fourth binomial (10.63).

**Step 7.** A binomial has only one division into its terms (10.42). Therefore the greater and lesser terms of this fourth binomial are precisely U and V, identified in Step 5. By the definition of a fourth binomial, U² exceeds V² by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with U (D10.2.4).

**Step 8.** The apotome U − V thus has its whole U commensurable in length with r, while U² exceeds the square on its annex V by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with U. It is therefore a fourth apotome (D10.3.4). By Step 4, it is exactly the breadth produced by applying the square on the given minor straight line to the given rational straight line. This proves the proposition.

heath_proof_text: Let AB be a minor and CD a rational straight line, and to the rational straight line CD let CE be applied equal to the square on AB and producing CF as breadth; I say that CF is a fourth apotome. For let BG be the annex to AB; therefore AG, GB are straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on AG, GB rational, but twice the rectangle AG, GB medial. [X. 76] To CD let there be applied CH equal to the square on AG and producing CK as breadth, and KL equal to the square on BG, producing KM as breadth; therefore the whole CL is equal to the squares on AG, GB. And the sum of the squares on AG, GB is rational; therefore CL is also rational. And it is applied to the rational straight line CD, producing CM as breadth; therefore CM is also rational and commensurable in length with CD. [X. 20] And, since the whole CL is equal to the squares on AG, GB, and, in these, CE is equal to the square on AB, therefore the remainder FL is equal to twice the rectangle AG, GB. [II. 7] Let then FM be bisected at the point N, and let NO be drawn through N parallel to either of the straight lines CD, ML; therefore each of the rectangles FO, NL is equal to the rectangle AG, GB. And, since twice the rectangle AG, GB is medial and is equal to FL, therefore FL is also medial. And it is applied to the rational straight line FE, producing FM as breadth; therefore FM is rational and incommensurable in length with CD. [X. 22] And, since the sum of the squares on AG, GB is rational, while twice the rectangle AG, GB is medial, the squares on AG, GB are incommensurable with twice the rectangle AG, GB. But CL is equal to the squares on AG, GB, and FL equal to twice the rectangle AG, GB; therefore CL is incommensurable with FL. But, as CL is to FL, so is CM to MF; [VI. 1] therefore CM is incommensurable in length with MF. [X. 11] And both are rational; therefore CM, MF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore CF is an apotome. [X. 73] I say that it is also a fourth apotome. For, since AG, GB are incommensurable in square, therefore the square on AG is also incommensurable with the square on GB. And CH is equal to the square on AG, and KL equal to the square on GB; therefore CH is incommensurable with KL. But, as CH is to KL, so is CK to KM; [VI. 1] therefore CK is incommensurable in length with KM. [X. 11] And, since the rectangle AG, GB is a mean proportional between the squares on AG, GB, and the square on AG is equal to CH, the square on GB to KL, and the rectangle AG, GB to NL, therefore NL is a mean proportional between CH, KL; therefore, as CH is to NL, so is NL to KL. But, as CH is to NL, so is CK to NM, and, as NL is to KL, so is NM to KM; [VI. 1] therefore, as CK is to MN, so is MN to KM; [V. 11] therefore the rectangle CK, KM is equal to the square on MN [VI. 17], that is, to the fourth part of the square on FM. Since then CM, MF are two unequal straight lines, and the rectangle CK, KM equal to the fourth part of the square on MF and deficient by a square figure has been applied to CM and divides it into incommensurable parts, therefore the square on CM is greater than the square on MF by the square on a straight line incommensurable with CM. [X. 18] And the whole CM is commensurable in length with the rational straight line CD set out; therefore CF is a fourth apotome. [X. Deff. III. 4]
